title: Work and energy transfer

learning_outcomes.text: understand the concept of work, and recall and use work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force

prior_knowledge_summary: 9702_t01_m01_o01: every physical quantity has a numerical magnitude and a unit.
9702_t01_m04_o01: force and displacement are vector quantities.
9702_t01_m04_o03: a vector can be represented as two perpendicular components.
new_learning: Work is an energy transfer caused when a force has a displacement component along its line of action.
The sign of work done by a force depends on the direction of that force relative to the displacement.
not_yet_taught: the principle of conservation of energy
the derivation or use of P = Fv
gravitational potential energy and ΔE_P = mgΔh
elastic strain energy and force-extension graph area

blocks.heading: Why does the wall receive no energy?
content: You push a rigid wall with a large steady force for ten seconds. Your arms become tired, but the wall does not move. Now use a much smaller force to slide a box across the floor. In which case has your force done mechanical work on the object?
The size of a force alone is not enough. Mechanical work needs both a force and displacement in the force direction. With no displacement of the wall, the work done on the wall is zero.

figure.purpose: Contrast a large force with zero displacement against a smaller force that produces displacement.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with two panels. Left: hands push a fixed wall, force arrow present, displacement labelled zero. Right: hands push a box that moves, with parallel force and displacement arrows. Use sparse coloured annotations.
figure.alt_text: A person pushes an unmoving wall in one panel and a moving box in another, comparing force and displacement.

blocks.heading: Work measures an energy transfer
content: When a force moves an object through a displacement, energy can be transferred. Pushing a crate can transfer energy from your body to the crate and its surroundings. A resisting force can transfer energy away from the moving object.
Definition to learn: product of force and displacement in the direction of the force.
The direction phrase matters. We must use the part of the displacement along the force, or equivalently the part of the force along the displacement.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: product of force and displacement in the direction of the force

figure.purpose: Link force-directed displacement to energy transfer without introducing later energy formulas.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper energy pathway sketch. Show a hand pushing a crate, a force arrow and matching displacement arrow, plus a simple energy-transfer arrow from person to crate and surroundings. Keep labels short.
figure.alt_text: A hand pushes a crate while parallel force and displacement arrows show an energy transfer.

blocks.heading: The formula to remember
content: Formula to remember: W = Fs.
Here W is work done in joules, J. F is the constant force, or the force component along the displacement, in newtons, N. s is the displacement in the direction of that force in metres, m.
One joule is one newton metre. This unit gives a quick check: multiplying N by m must produce J.

controlled_formula.name: Work done by a constant force

figure.purpose: Make the force, displacement and unit relationship visible in one compact representation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated formula card. Place W = Fs centrally, with a small box-and-arrow sketch and branches to W in J, F in N and s in m. Include 1 J = 1 N m.
figure.alt_text: An annotated W equals F s formula card links work in joules to force in newtons and displacement in metres.

blocks.heading: A force along the motion
content: A warehouse tug exerts a constant horizontal force of 210 N while a trolley moves 8.0 m horizontally.
The force and displacement are parallel, so the whole 210 N force contributes. Use W = Fs = 210 × 8.0 = 1680 J. To two significant figures, W = 1.7 × 10^3 J.
Check the scale: 200 N acting through about 8 m should give about 1600 J, so 1680 J is sensible. Check the unit separately: N × m = J.

figure.purpose: Show the complete knowns-to-substitution route for direct work calculation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout. Show a trolley with 210 N and 8.0 m parallel arrows, then W = Fs, substitution, answer and two small check boxes for scale and units.
figure.alt_text: A trolley calculation uses a 210 newton force through 8.0 metres to obtain 1680 joules.

blocks.heading: Direction changes the work
content: If force and displacement point in the same direction, the force does positive work. If they are perpendicular, the displacement in the force direction is zero, so that force does zero work. A support force on a tray carried horizontally is an example.
If a force points opposite to the displacement, it does negative work. For a 40 N resistive force acting while an object moves 6.0 m, work done by the resistive force is W = -40 × 6.0 = -240 J.

Cambridge questions often ask for work done against resistance. That phrase asks for the positive energy-transfer magnitude, 240 J in this example. Read whether the question asks for work done by the resisting force or work done against it.

figure.purpose: Compare positive, zero and negative work through force-displacement direction.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper three-column comparison. Same box moves right in every column. Force points right for positive work, up for zero work and left for negative work. Include only signs and short direction labels.
figure.alt_text: Three force diagrams compare positive, zero and negative work for the same rightward displacement.

blocks.heading: An angled pull uses only its parallel component
content: A rope pulls a sled with force 125 N at 35 degrees above horizontal. The sled moves 18 m horizontally. Resolve the force along the displacement first: F_parallel = 125 cos 35 degrees = 102.4 N.
Now use the controlled work formula with that component: W = F_parallel s = 102.4 × 18 = 1843 J. To three significant figures, W = 1.84 × 10^3 J.

The vertical force component is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so it does zero work. An independent limit check also helps: the answer must be less than 125 × 18 = 2250 J because only part of the force is parallel.

figure.purpose: Teach the two-stage component then work procedure for an angled force.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked vector sketch. Draw a sled, a 125 N rope at 35 degrees, an 18 m horizontal displacement and dashed horizontal and vertical components. Beside it show the two calculation stages and the less-than-2250 J check.
figure.alt_text: An angled 125 newton pull is resolved horizontally before calculating work over 18 metres.

blocks.heading: Force times any distance is not enough
content: It can feel natural to multiply the force by the full path length every time. That works only when the force is along the displacement. The shortcut fails for a carried tray, an angled cable or a resisting force because direction changes the contributing displacement.
Repair the method with three questions. What displacement occurred? Which component of the force lies along it? Does that component point with the displacement, across it or against it?
A second common error is using the vertical component of an angled pull for horizontal motion. Sketching one horizontal displacement arrow makes the needed component visible.

figure.purpose: Repair the habit of multiplying total force by path length without checking direction.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error-correction flow. Cross out a total-force-times-distance shortcut for an angled pull, then show three checkpoints: displacement, parallel component, direction sign. End with W = Fs using the parallel component.
figure.alt_text: An error-correction flow replaces total force times distance with a direction and component check.

blocks.heading: Reverse the formula and combine force contributions
content: If 840 J is transferred by work against a constant resistance over 7.0 m, rearrange W = Fs to F = W/s. The resistance magnitude is 840/7.0 = 120 N. Multiplying back, 120 × 7.0 = 840 J, checks the result.
Now suppose a worker pushes with 160 N while a 40 N resistance acts opposite the motion over 10 m. The worker does +1600 J. Resistance does -400 J. The total work by these two forces is +1200 J.
Keep the contributions separate until their signs are clear. This avoids subtracting when the question asks only for work done by the driving force, or adding when it asks for total work.

blocks.heading: A reliable work checklist
content: First identify the force whose work is requested and the object's displacement. Next find the force component along that displacement. Use W = Fs with metres and newtons.

Then attach meaning to the sign. Same direction gives positive work, perpendicular gives zero work and opposite direction gives negative work. Work done against resistance is usually reported as a positive magnitude.

Finally check units, scale and wording. This lesson stops at work and energy transfer by a force. The rules for conservation, efficiency, power, gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy come later.

concepts_taught: work as energy transferred by a force acting through displacement
work done against resistance as a positive magnitude
direct and reverse use of W = Fs
misconceptions_addressed: A large force must do work even when there is no displacement.
The total force can always be multiplied by the path length without checking direction.
The vertical component of an angled pull contributes to work during horizontal displacement.
Work done by resistance and work done against resistance have the same sign.
next_lesson_can_assume: The accepted definition of work done.
Direct and reverse use of W = Fs for a constant force.
Selection of the force component parallel to displacement.
Interpretation of positive, zero and negative work by direction.
One joule is one newton metre.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: The principle of conservation of energy.
Gravitational potential energy or kinetic energy formulas.
Elastic strain energy or gas expansion work.
